span.label: A LITERATURE GRADED AGAINST A PUBLISHED CHECKLIST, AND THE ATTRITION IS ITEMISED RATHER THAN SCORED. 25 studies reviewed; `Thirteen of the 25 studies provided strong evidence of rigorous research across the four categories of the essential QIs`; and `Quotation withheld.` **25 to 13 to 8**, with each drop attributable to a named criterion rather than to a composite score. That is the `tool must be checkable` principle applied to a whole field: external criteria, per-criterion grading, failures named
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: AND THE MISSING INDICATORS ARE NAMED ONE BY ONE, WHICH IS WHAT MAKES THE REVIEW ACTIONABLE: one study `failed to provide sufficient information on teachers delivering the intervention`; of the eight high-quality studies `ONLY FIVE ... also documented that data collectors were BLIND TO CONDITIONS`; only one `provided information on the QUALITY OF IMPLEMENTATION`; and **`Quotation withheld`** - a zero across all 25. A reviewer reading this knows exactly what the next study should add, which a quality SCORE would not have told them
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: THE VERDICT IS EXPLICITLY RELATIVE TO ITS CRITERIA: `Quotation withheld.` **The qualifier is inside the claim.** `Evidence-based` is not asserted as a property of the practice but as the output of a named, published standard - so a reader who rejects the standard knows exactly what they are rejecting, and a different standard could give a different answer without either party being wrong about the studies
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: quality indicators —operationalised-as→ evidence-based practices
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — **THE `BY APPLYING` IS THE WHOLE EDGE AND IT IS IN THE QUOTE.** `Evidence-based practice` here is not a property discovered in the world but the output of applying a named checklist, and the paper says so in the sentence that makes the claim. Weight 0.9. This is the cleanest `operationalised-as` I have tagged: the construct and its operational definition are in one clause, and the definition is external and citable.

span.label: instructional approach (schema-based / visual representation)
span.note: retracted: RE-GROUNDED, AND THE REPLACEMENT USES DIFFERENT WORDS THAN THE TITLE ON PURPOSE. The evidence was a substring of the paper's own title, 'Quotation withheld'. **The phrase `schema-based instruction` occurs ZERO times in the staged body**: `schema` appears 10 times, once as a diagram type in a list ('strip or tape, schema, percentage bar') and otherwise as `schematic representations`, never as the named approach the title advertises. So the variable is real and the paper discusses it under the word `schematic`; this span is the paper contrasting the two representation types the variable ranges over. A title naming a construct the body never names is also a truncation signal and is flagged as one. See Q-716.
Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.
